gapFill.title: Fill in the gap
gapFill.subtitle: Type the whole verb phrase — the past simple or the present perfect, whichever the signal word or context calls for. Twenty original sentences.

questions.explain: 'In 2019' is a finished time — use the past simple.
No specific time — an experience, so use the present perfect.
'Since 2020' with a situation that continues — present perfect.

questions.after: you arrive? Was the flight OK?
questions.explain: 'When' asks for a specific time — it takes the past simple.

wordOrder.title: Put the words in order

matching.title: Match the signal word to the tense
matching.subtitle: Tap a signal word or phrase, then tap the tense it forces. A finished time takes the past simple; an unspecified time or a link to now takes the present perfect.

timedMC.title: Beat the clock
timedMC.subtitle: 15 seconds per question. The signal word decides the tense — a finished time takes the past simple; an unspecified time or a link to now takes the present perfect.

questions.text: The Titanic        in 1912.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: 'in 1912' is a finished time — use the past simple, not the present perfect.
Wrong tense and form: 'in 1912' needs the past simple — and the participle is 'sunk', not 'sank'.
Wrong tense: this needs the past simple, not the present simple.
questions.explain: 'In 1912' is a finished time — past simple.

questions.text: My brother        three marathons in his life, and he wants to run another one.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: 'in his life' is not finished — he's still running — so use the present perfect, not the past simple.
Wrong form: after 'has', use the participle 'run', not 'ran'.
Wrong tense: this is his experience up to now — the present perfect, not the present simple.
questions.explain: Experience up to now ('in his life', and he still runs) — present perfect.

questions.text: When        you buy that jacket?
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: 'when' asks for a specific time — it takes the past simple, not the present perfect.
Wrong tense and agreement: 'when' takes the past simple — and 'you' never takes 'has'.
Wrong auxiliary: 'are' can't go with the base verb 'buy' — 'when' needs 'did'.
questions.explain: 'When' asks for a specific time — past simple: 'When did you buy…?'

questions.text: Lucy        her best friend since nursery school.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: 'since' with a friendship that continues needs the present perfect, not the past simple.
Wrong tense: 'since' links the past to now — the present simple can't do that.
Wrong form: 'know' isn't used in the continuous, and 'since' needs the present perfect.
questions.explain: 'Since nursery school' with a situation that continues — present perfect.

questions.text: Oh no! Somebody        my bike — it isn't here!
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: the result is here now (the bike is missing) — use the present perfect, not the past simple.
Subject-verb agreement: with 'somebody', use 'has', not 'have'.
Wrong tense: this needs the present perfect, not the present simple.
questions.explain: A recent action with a result now (no bike!) — present perfect.

questions.text: We        camping in the mountains last weekend.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: 'last weekend' is a finished time — use the past simple, not the present perfect.
Wrong tense: this needs the past simple, not the present simple.
Wrong tense: 'last weekend' is a finished time — use the past simple, not the present perfect continuous.
questions.explain: 'Last weekend' is a finished time — past simple.

questions.text: My uncle        a mobile phone — he says he doesn't need one.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: he's still alive and still has no phone — 'never' up to now needs the present perfect, not the past simple.
Wrong tense and agreement: this needs the present perfect, and 'my uncle' takes 'has'.
Subject-verb agreement: with 'my uncle', use 'has', not 'have'.
questions.explain: 'Never' up to now — present perfect.

questions.text: Look! The cat        all the milk — the bowl is empty.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: 'Look!' + a result you can see now (an empty bowl) needs the present perfect, not the past simple.
Wrong form: after 'has', use the participle 'drunk', not the past simple 'drank'.
Wrong tense: this needs the present perfect, not the present simple.
questions.explain: A recent action with a visible result now — present perfect.

questions.text: I        a really strange dream last night.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: 'last night' is a finished time — use the past simple, not the present perfect.
Wrong tense and agreement: 'last night' needs the past simple — and 'I' never takes 'has'.
Wrong tense: this needs the past simple, not the present simple.
questions.explain: 'Last night' is a finished time — past simple.

questions.text: Don't take the plates away — Sam        his dinner yet.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: in British English, 'yet' signals the present perfect, even in the negative.
Subject-verb agreement: with 'Sam', use 'hasn't', not 'haven't'.
Wrong tense: 'yet' needs the present perfect, not the present simple.
questions.explain: 'Yet' signals the present perfect, even negative.

questions.text: My parents        married for thirty years, and they're still happy.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: they are still married — 'for thirty years' up to now needs the present perfect, not the past simple.
Wrong tense: 'for thirty years' up to now needs the present perfect, not the present simple.
Subject-verb agreement: with 'my parents', use 'have', not 'has'.
questions.explain: 'For thirty years' with a situation that continues — present perfect.

questions.text: your dad ever cooked dinner for the whole family?
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: 'ever' asks about experience up to now — present perfect, not past simple (and 'cooked' would be 'cook').
Subject-verb agreement: with 'your dad', use 'has', not 'have'.
Wrong tense: 'ever' + 'cooked' needs the present perfect, not the present simple.
questions.explain: 'Ever' signals the present perfect: 'Has your dad ever cooked…?'

questions.text: Don't cook tonight — Mum        a pizza already.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: in British English, 'already' signals the present perfect, not the past simple.
Subject-verb agreement: with 'Mum', use 'has', not 'have'.
Wrong tense: 'already' needs the present perfect, not the present simple.
questions.explain: 'Already' signals the present perfect.

questions.text: My friend        me a message ten minutes ago.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: 'ago' names a finished time — use the past simple, not the present perfect.
Wrong tense and agreement: 'ago' needs the past simple — and 'my friend' would take 'has'.
Wrong tense: this needs the past simple, not the present simple.
questions.explain: 'Ago' names a finished time — past simple.

questions.text: Be careful — I        the floor, and it's still wet.
wrongReasons: Subject-verb agreement: with 'I', use 'have', not 'has'.
Wrong form: after 'have', use the participle 'cleaned', not the base verb 'clean'.
Wrong tense: the floor is wet now because of a very recent action — present perfect with 'just', not the present simple.
questions.explain: 'Just' + a result now (the wet floor) — present perfect.

questions.text: Mozart        his first piece of music when he was five.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: 'when he was five' is a finished time — use the past simple, not the present perfect.
Wrong tense and form: this needs the past simple — and the participle would be 'written', not 'wrote'.
Wrong tense: this needs the past simple, not the present simple.
questions.explain: 'When he was five' is a finished time — past simple.

questions.text: It        for three weeks, and the garden is very dry.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: 'for three weeks' up to now (the garden is still dry) needs the present perfect, even negative.
Wrong tense: 'for three weeks' up to now needs the present perfect, not the present simple.
Subject-verb agreement: with 'it', use 'hasn't', not 'haven't'.
questions.explain: 'For three weeks' up to now — present perfect, even in the negative.

questions.text: My team        the final last Saturday.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: 'last Saturday' is a finished time — use the past simple, not the present perfect.
Wrong tense: 'last Saturday' is a finished time — use the past simple, not the present perfect.
Wrong tense: this needs the past simple, not the present simple.
questions.explain: 'Last Saturday' is a finished time — past simple.

questions.text: She        in Paris since 2015.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: 'since 2015' with a continuing situation needs the present perfect, not the past simple.
Subject-verb agreement: with 'she', use 'has', not 'have'.
Wrong tense: 'since' with a continuing situation needs the present perfect, not the present continuous.
questions.explain: 'Since 2015' with a continuing situation — present perfect.

questions.text: Sorry, I        your call last night — my phone was off.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: 'last night' is a finished time — use the past simple, even negative.
